doc.title: Phil Flanigan interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

chapter: Life in New York and session work
title: Why he could not play repetitive pit parts
summary: He is too restless to repeat the same bass line.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Oh, by all means. They do financially better than us a lot of the time, just by virtue of the fact that it’s steady work. It may not pay that great per night or whatever, but over the course of the year they’re probably making more than we are because they’re working five, six, seven, eight gigs a week. Like the guys that were in that show “Cats” and there are several other long running shows in New York with pit bands. These guys, they know their parts so well, they play it the same way every night, that they’re reading magazines, mixing herb formulas, and packing their pipe for the intermission, and all this stuff, and © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -15-

then the note comes — toot — you know, they’re reading something and preparing something and then [scats] like that. And they go along with whatever they were doing, and Chapter 6, let’s see, five, four, three, two, [scats]. And then that’s it. It’s funny to watch these guys. I don’t envy them, because I’m mentally too restless. I mean I can’t even handle a repeating bass line for more than about eight bars. That’s agony for me, to have to repeat the same thing over and over. It’s like talking to you like, like talking to you like, like talking to you like—
Like talking to you like this. I mean—

It’s got to flow. Yeah, I know a lot of people that are on loops. You ever know someone on a real short loop? How long can you take that? You hang out with a person, and in ten minutes you start hearing the same stories over and over. That’s a ten minute loop hard wired in.
